strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important problem: KV cache memory overhead for long-CoT reasoning LLMs, where existing short-context KV quantization methods demonstrably fail (e.g., near-0% accuracy for some baselines at 2-bit).

Well-motivated technical analysis: the RoPE low-frequency channel argument for why short calibration data fails is clear and quantitatively supported (e.g., a 54,410-token period for the lowest-frequency channel in DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B).

The proposed combination (progressive bit-width shrinking via an equivalent right-shift operation, ILP-based block-wise bit allocation, and positional-interpolation-based calibration) is coherent, and each component is individually ablated (Tables 3, 4; Figures 2-4).
Fairly broad evaluation across model scales (7B to 70B), multiple reasoning benchmarks (AIME-2024/2025, CMIMC, LiveCodeBench), with repeated sampling, mean/std reporting, and voting accuracy.
weaknesses: All experiments use fake quantization on GPUs; there is no real-system implementation, no latency/throughput measurement, and no accounting for the runtime cost of repeated dequantize-requantize bit-width shrinking operations during decoding. For a systems-oriented contribution, this is a significant gap.

Comparison fairness is questionable: baselines are evaluated at batch sizes chosen so 'all methods fully utilize memory,' but the effective memory budgets and configurations across rows (e.g., KIVI BS=32/40 vs. PM-KVQ BS=32 with 2/4-bit mixed precision) are confusing and not rigorously controlled, making the headline 'up to 8%' gain hard to attribute cleanly.

The core ideas are incremental relative to prior work: progressive/deferred quantization is a known technique in weight quantization, sliding-window FP16 retention and first-token INT16 are directly adopted from KIVI, Taylor-based sensitivity + ILP mixed-precision allocation is standard (LLM-MQ, MixQ), and positional interpolation is borrowed as-is; the novelty lies mainly in the specific composition and the right-shift shrinking trick.

The claimed benefit of positional-interpolation calibration is thin: the ablation shows only a 1.66% pass@1 gain, s=16 actually degrades performance, and the method assumes PI-transformed short-data distributions match real long-sequence distributions — the calibration data (arXiv papers) also may not match long-CoT generation distributions. No long-context task (e.g., LongBench/needle-in-haystack) is used to validate the long-context distribution claim directly.

Several methods, including the proposed one, sometimes underperform the 16-bit baseline (e.g., QwQ-32B voting on AIME-2024, PM-KVQ 2/4-bit), and the paper does not discuss when/why the method degrades.

Missing strong recent baselines relevant to the setting (e.g., SKVQ, WKVQuant); RotateKV, the strongest 2-bit competitor, is only partially evaluated (fails on some models, and only on Qwen-7B/LLaMA-8B in Table 2).

Reproducibility is undermined: the code link in the abstract is empty ('available at .'), and some details (e.g., exact memory budgets per configuration, how the 16-bit headroom interacts with variable-length generations) are under-specified.
Acknowledged limitations are substantial: no MLA support (excluding DeepSeek-V3-style models, arguably the most relevant modern long-CoT LLMs), and no integration with real inference engines.

strengths: The paper targets a timely and practically important problem: KV cache memory overhead in long-CoT reasoning LLMs, which is indeed a real deployment bottleneck.

The proposed system combines three reasonable components (progressive bit-width shrinking, block-wise mixed-precision allocation via integer programming, and positional-interpolation-based calibration), and the 'Equivalent Right Shift' re-quantization operator is a concrete technical contribution.

Evaluation covers a reasonably broad model range (7B to 70B) across several reasoning and code benchmarks, with vote-based accuracy, standard deviations, and ablation studies for the main design choices.
Code availability is claimed, supporting reproducibility of the algorithmic side.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: each component is a straightforward adaptation of known ideas — progressive quantization is essentially memory-budget-triggered bit-width shrinking; block-wise mixed precision via first-order Taylor sensitivity plus an integer program closely follows prior mixed-precision work (LLM-MQ, MixDQ, MiKV); positional interpolation is reused verbatim from Chen et al. [3]. The paper reads as an engineering combination rather than a new methodological insight.

Evaluation uses 'fake quantization' only. There is no real quantized kernel, no measured memory savings, throughput, or latency, so the central practical claim (making low-bit KV cache viable under memory budgets) is not validated in an actual system. For a systems-flavored efficiency paper this is a significant gap.

Baseline comparisons raise fairness concerns: the authors explicitly choose bit-widths that 'lead to significant performance degradation when using baseline methods,' and batch sizes/GPU targets differ across configurations, making the headline 'up to 8%' improvement hard to interpret as an apples-to-apples comparison.

Statistical rigor is weak: AIME contains only 30 problems per year, and several claimed gains (e.g., the 0.84% additional gain from block-wise allocation, or the 1.66% gain from positional interpolation) are well within reported confidence intervals. The positional-interpolation benefit is demonstrated on a single model only and reverses at s=16, undermining the generality of the calibration claim.

The 'large cumulative error' motivation is asserted but never analyzed quantitatively (no error accumulation measurements, no perplexity or long-context evaluations), and the paper does not compare against non-quantization baselines such as KV eviction or sliding-window attention, which may be more natural competitors under the same memory budget.

Inconsistencies and incomplete details: CMIMC-2025 in the text vs. CMIMC-2024 in Table 2; Equation (3) is presented without derivation or correctness argument; the block-allocation IP is essentially a small knapsack trivially solvable in closed form, so framing it as integer programming overstates the contribution; MLA models are excluded, which limits applicability to modern reasoning models.

PM-KVQ generally remains below the 16-bit model on most benchmarks, and the paper does not carefully discuss when the method is truly lossless vs. merely less degraded, which matters for deployment claims.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated problem: KV cache memory overhead is a genuine bottleneck for long-CoT reasoning LLMs, and the paper clearly identifies two concrete failure modes (cumulative quantization error and RoPE-induced miscalibration of low-frequency channels) that prior short-context methods do not address.

The progressive quantization idea is sensible and well-motivated: the observation that fixed low-bit quantization under-utilizes the memory budget at the start of decoding is correct, and the 'Equivalent Right Shift' bit-width shrinking trick is a neat, non-obvious engineering contribution supported by a dedicated ablation (Table 3).

Comprehensive evaluation for the area: five long-CoT models spanning 7B–70B, four recent reasoning benchmarks (AIME-2024/2025, CMIMC-2025, LiveCodeBench), competitive SOTA baselines (KIVI, MiKV, RotateKV) with std across sampled responses, and ablations of each proposed component.

Block-wise allocation is cleanly formalized as a memory-constrained integer program using first-order Taylor sensitivity, and the sensitivity analysis in Appendix B yields interpretable findings (e.g., first-block sensitivity in Qwen-based models, deeper blocks more sensitive).
The positional-interpolation calibration is an elegant zero-overhead solution to the RoPE channel-coverage problem, with an ablation showing it recovers the accuracy of 4x-longer calibration data.
Honest reporting: the limitations (MLA not supported, no system-level integration) and broader impacts are explicitly discussed.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: each component is a recombination of established techniques — sliding window and first-token INT16 retention are taken directly from KIVI/SKVQ, block-wise mixed precision via sensitivity is standard (LLM-MQ, MixDQ), and positional interpolation is borrowed from Chen et al. The main novelty is applying them in the long-CoT setting and the shifting-based shrinking rule.

All experiments use fake quantization on a single server; there is no real kernel implementation, no measured wall-clock speedup, effective throughput, or real memory savings, so the practical system-level value of the method is unverified. The authors acknowledge this but it substantially weakens the significance of the contribution.

The 'cumulative error' motivation is asserted rather than directly measured: no token-level error curves, perplexity trajectories, or degradation-vs-length analyses are provided to substantiate that progressive quantization reduces cumulative error as opposed to merely amortizing memory.

Comparison fairness is muddled by varying batch sizes across methods and configurations (e.g., PM-KVQ BS=32 vs KIVI BS=40 for Qwen-7B), making some head-to-head numbers difficult to interpret; the memory-budget accounting across the different (BS, Fbit) configurations should be stated more precisely.

Generalization is narrow: essentially one model lineage (DeepSeek-R1-Distill family plus QwQ-32B, which is also Qwen-based). No non-reasoning long-context evaluation (e.g., RULER/LongBench) to test whether the method helps or hurts general long-context tasks, and no other model families with different RoPE/attention designs.

Ablations are limited to a single model (DeepSeek-LLaMA-8B) and small effect sizes: the positional interpolation gain (1.66% pass@1 on 30-problem AIME) is within plausible sampling noise, and s=16 degrading performance suggests the approach is heuristic without a principled way to choose s.
The sensitivity metric uses gradients computed on short calibration data, which may not reflect sensitivity during 32K-token generation; this mismatch is not analyzed.

Technical sloppiness: Eq. (3) is stated without derivation or verification of its equivalence claim; the claim that CVXPY solves the integer program 'within a few seconds' is imprecise (CVXPY is a convex modeling layer and requires an external MIP solver); benchmark sizes (30 problems per AIME year) make several of the headline deltas statistically fragile.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practical problem: KV cache memory overhead in long-CoT reasoning LLMs (32K+ token generations), where existing short-context quantization methods indeed break down.

The core observation that existing methods underutilize the memory budget (storing fixed low-bit cache even when memory is free) is well-motivated, and progressive quantization with bit-width shrinking to exploit this is a sensible solution.

The 'Equivalent Right Shift' bit-width shrinking operation is technically clean, with a full correctness proof in Appendix D and a convincing ablation (Table 4) showing it substantially outperforms naive shifting strategies.

The positional-interpolation-based calibration trick is clever: it approximates long-context RoPE channel distributions with short calibration data at no extra cost, with an ablation (Table 5) supporting the choice of scaling factor s=4.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 5 models spanning 7B–70B, multiple benchmarks (AIME, CMIMC, LiveCodeBench, IFEval), comparisons against strong recent baselines (KIVI, RotateKV, MiKV, KVTuner), multiple batch-size/GPU configurations, throughput analysis, sensitivity analysis across blocks, and integration with sparse attention (QuestAttention) in the appendix.
The paper is generally well-written and reproducible, with code release, detailed experimental settings, and an honest ethics/limitations discussion.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental. Each component builds heavily on prior art: the sliding window and INT16 first-token schemes are adopted from KIVI; layer-wise mixed-precision allocation via Taylor sensitivity closely resembles KVTuner and general mixed-precision quantization; positional interpolation is a direct reuse of Chen et al. (2023). The main new ideas (quantize progressively as memory fills; a fixed integer-shift re-quantization formula) are more engineering than conceptual advances.

The 'large cumulative error' framing is somewhat overstated: the claimed error accumulation across decoding steps is not formally characterized or measured (no error-growth analysis, perplexity curves, or token-level divergence statistics), and the alternative explanation (memory underutilization) conflates two different phenomena.

Benchmark sizes are small and noisy: AIME-2024/2025 have only 30 problems each, and several headline gains (e.g., the 0.84% extra gain from block-wise allocation at BS=32) are within the reported standard deviations (±4–7%), making the significance of some comparisons questionable. No statistical significance testing is provided.

Fairness of comparisons is debatable: PM-KVQ temporarily stores the KV cache at higher bit-width (16/8/4-bit) before shrinking, so during early decoding it uses more memory/precision than baselines; the throughput comparison with KIVI also relies on custom 16/8-bit kernels whose implementation quality could affect results. The C.3 comparison truncates KIVI outputs when memory is exhausted, which is a somewhat artificial protocol.

Efficiency claims are weaker than accuracy claims: PM-KVQ has 2.45–16.18% throughput degradation versus KIVI, and the pre-inference cost grows for larger models (120 min for 70B); end-to-end serving metrics (e.g., latency under concurrent load) are not evaluated.

Generality is limited: only DeepSeek-R1-Distill and QwQ models (all GQA, RoPE-based) are tested; MLA models and non-distilled long-CoT models are excluded (acknowledged in limitations), and the method's dependence on known maximum output length for budget computation may not hold in open-ended serving scenarios.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and timely problem: KV cache memory overhead in long-CoT reasoning LLMs, where prior short-context quantization methods demonstrably fail (e.g., RotateKV/MiKV producing 0.00 accuracy at 2-bit).

Comprehensive empirical coverage: five long-CoT models from 7B to 70B, four benchmarks (AIME-2024/2025, CMIMC-2024, LiveCodeBench) plus IFEval, multiple batch-size and GPU configurations, and comparisons with several SOTA baselines including KVTuner in the appendix.

Well-executed ablations: the three bit-width shrinking strategies are compared (Table 4), sensitivity analysis across all blocks is shown (Figures 3-4), and the positional interpolation scaling factor is studied (Table 5).
The 'Equivalent Right Shift' requantization scheme is clean and accompanied by a full correctness proof (Appendix D), which is more rigor than many quantization papers provide.

Efficiency analysis includes real CUDA kernels, throughput measurements, and pre-inference calibration latency (Tables 3 and 11), and code release plus reproducibility statement support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: each component is a relatively straightforward combination of existing ideas. Progressive quantization is essentially staged requantization; block-wise mixed-precision allocation closely overlaps prior work (KVTuner already does sensitivity-aware layer-wise mixed-precision KV quantization; MiKV does token-level mixed precision); positional interpolation is borrowed directly from Chen et al. (2023) and applied to calibration. The framing as three new techniques overstates the conceptual contribution.

The headline gains for individual components are small and possibly within noise: block-wise memory allocation adds only ~0.84% and positional interpolation only ~1.66% on AIME-2024, while the reported standard deviations on these 30-problem benchmarks are ±4-7%. The main benefit appears to come from the progressive scheme (i.e., simply using more bits for early tokens), which weakens the significance of the more 'novel' components.

Evaluation on small, high-variance benchmarks: AIME-2024/2025 and CMIMC contain ~30 problems each, and pass@1 differences of 1-3% are not clearly statistically significant; the 70B model is evaluated only on AIME-2024, further limiting evidence at scale.

The motivating claim that existing methods 'waste memory' is somewhat misleading: at maximum context length, uniform-bit methods use the full budget; the waste only occurs for shorter generations, so the benefit of progressive quantization is conditional on the response-length distribution (partially acknowledged in C.8 but not confronted honestly in the main narrative).

Accuracy results are obtained with fake quantization; only throughput uses real kernels. The interaction between progressive shrinking and real kernel accuracy/latency (e.g., mixed-precision attention over caches at different bit-widths) is not validated end-to-end.

Throughput comparisons are confounded: PM-KVQ and KIVI are evaluated at much larger batch sizes (110/4) than the FP16 baseline (18/1), and the 2.73-5.18x speedup largely reflects memory savings from any 2-bit scheme rather than the specific contributions.

Fixed hyperparameters (s=4, group size 128, grid-searched alpha) are presented without sensitivity analysis in the main text, and the method is restricted to GQA-style models, excluding MLA architectures that are increasingly standard in long-context reasoning LLMs.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: KV cache quantization for long-CoT reasoning LLMs is timely and practically important, and the paper clearly identifies two concrete failure modes (cumulative quantization error and short-context calibration under RoPE) that existing short-context methods suffer from.

The three proposed techniques are coherent and well-integrated: progressive quantization with a formally proven 'Equivalent Right Shift' strategy (Appendix D), block-wise bit-width allocation formalized as an Integer Programming problem with Taylor-estimated sensitivities, and positional-interpolation-based calibration that increases effective calibration length at no extra cost.

Extensive empirical evaluation: 5 models from 7B to 70B, comparisons against multiple strong baselines (KIVI, RotateKV, MiKV, KVTuner), plus ablations for each component, efficiency/throughput analysis, multiple GPU configurations, short-context (IFEval) generalization, and integration with sparse attention (QuestAttention).
Results are meaningful: up to 8% improvements over SOTA at 2-bit settings where baselines collapse (e.g., RotateKV/MiKV produce 0.00), and demonstrated 2.73-5.18x throughput over 16-bit inference.

Reasonable reproducibility: calibration data, hyperparameters (s=4, alpha grid search, group size 128), batch size setups, and latency of the pre-inference pipeline are described in detail, with code release promised.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of individual components: progressive bit-width shrinking is a natural engineering extension, positional interpolation is directly borrowed from Chen et al. (2023), and Taylor-sensitivity-based integer programming for mixed-precision allocation is standard practice from prior mixed-precision quantization work. Layer-wise mixed-precision KV quantization also already exists (KVTuner), and the head-to-head comparison with KVTuner is limited to a single 7B model.

Statistical significance is a concern: the main benchmarks are tiny (AIME has 30 problems per year; CMIMC ~30), and several headline claims fall within the reported error bars (e.g., PM-KVQ 40.21±5.71 vs. 16-bit baseline 41.04±6.74 on AIME-2024; some QwQ-32B and 14B comparisons are within ±2-4%). The abstract's 'up to 8%' improvement should be contextualized against this variance.

All accuracy results use fake quantization on 8xA100 hardware; real quantized execution is only verified for 7B/32B throughput with KIVI-style kernels. Consistency between the fake-quantization accuracy pipeline and the deployed kernels (especially the new 16/8-bit and bit-shrinking kernels) is not validated end-to-end.

The memory-budget comparison framing is somewhat circular: PM-KVQ's advantage comes largely from being allowed to temporarily store higher-precision cache, and comparisons at different batch sizes (32 vs. 40, 12 vs. 16) make some rows difficult to interpret; notably, in Table 2 the uniform 2-bit PM-KVQ (BS=16) sometimes outperforms the mixed 2/4-bit variant, which is counterintuitive and unexplained.

The positional interpolation calibration uses effective length 8K while inference runs to 32K outputs; the paper does not justify why 8K effective calibration suffices, and the ablation showing degradation at s=16 suggests the approach's scope is narrow, but the boundary conditions are not analyzed.

Writing/presentation issues: the abstract's code URL is cut off, there are typos ('memory memory', 'can indeed performance drop'), and discrepancies exist between the reported gains and what the tables strictly support in a few places.
